topics.title: Meaning and Basic Features of Process Costing
explain: Process Costing is used in industries where raw material passes through two or more continuous processes to become a final product.
The finished output of one process becomes the raw material input for the next process until completion.
Costs are accumulated process-wise and averaged over total units produced during the period.
End products are standardized, homogeneous, and indistinguishable from one another.

flow.title: Continuous Flow of Material in Process Costing

topics.example: Sugar manufacturing where sugarcane is crushed into juice in Process I, boiled into syrup in Process II, and crystallized into sugar bags in Process III.
remember: Useful for continuous production like steel, paper, chemical, and oil refining industries.
mistakes: Confusing process costing with job costing, which is used for custom, non-continuous orders.

quiz.q: Which type of industry is best suited for Process Costing?
quiz.why: Process costing is designed for continuous, standardized manufacturing processes like chemical production.

quiz.q: In process costing, the output of Process-I becomes:
quiz.why: The completed output of a preceding process serves as the input material for the subsequent process.

topics.title: Costing Procedure in Process Costing
explain: A separate Process Account is opened for each individual manufacturing process.
Each account is debited with Direct Materials, Direct Labour, Direct Expenses, and apportioned Overheads.
Production overheads are collected and apportioned across processes using a suitable basis like direct wages.
The total accumulated cost of a process is transferred to credit side and debited to the next process account.

flow.title: Posting Costs in a Process Account

topics.example: Apportioning factory indirect expenses of ₹85,000 among three processes based on their direct labor wage ratio.
remember: Process Account is debited with inputs and expenses, and credited with transfers and scrap values.
mistakes: Forgetting to include the cost of output transferred from the previous process when debiting the next process.

quiz.q: Indirect production overheads are generally debited to process accounts on the basis of:
o: A pre-determined or suitable basis like direct wages
Equal division regardless of process size
quiz.why: Overheads cannot be traced directly, so they are apportioned using a suitable basis such as direct wage ratio.

quiz.q: Which side of the Process Account records the materials introduced and wages paid?
quiz.why: All costs and resources consumed in a process are debited to that specific Process Account.

topics.title: Treatment of Normal Loss, Abnormal Loss, and Abnormal Gain
explain: Normal Loss is inherent and expected under normal operating conditions; good units absorb its cost.
Scrap value realized from normal loss units is credited to the Process Account to reduce overall cost.
Abnormal Loss is unexpected loss exceeding normal loss; it is valued like good units and charged to Costing P&L.
Abnormal Gain occurs when actual output exceeds expected output; it is debited to Process Account and credited to Costing P&L.

flow.title: Evaluating Loss and Gain in a Process
steps: Compare Expected Production with Actual Output
Record Abnormal Loss or Abnormal Gain

topics.example: Inputs of 5,000 units with 5% normal loss (250 units). If actual output is 4,550 units, abnormal loss is 200 units.
remember: Unit Cost = (Total Cost - Realisable Value of Normal Loss) / (Total Input Units - Normal Loss Units).
mistakes: Valuing normal loss at the full cost per unit instead of its scrap realisable value.

quiz.q: How is the cost of Normal Process Loss treated in cost accounts?
o: Debited directly to Costing Profit and Loss Account
Absorbed by the good units produced in the process
Charged as an overhead to administrative department
quiz.why: Normal loss is inherent and unavoidable, so its net cost is absorbed by good units.

quiz.q: Abnormal Process Loss is calculated as:
o: Loss in excess of normal expected loss
Total units input minus normal loss
Total sales value minus scrap value
quiz.why: Abnormal loss represents any loss occurring over and above the pre-determined normal loss.

topics.title: Valuation of Work-in-Process & Equivalent Units
explain: In continuous manufacturing, incomplete units remain at the end of an accounting period (WIP).
Equivalent units represent incomplete units converted into equivalent fully completed units.
Percentage of completion is estimated separately for materials, labour, and overheads.
Equivalent Units = Actual number of incomplete units × Percentage of work completed.

flow.title: Calculation of Equivalent Units
steps: Assess Degree of Completion (%) per Cost Element
Multiply Physical Units by Completion Percentage
Sum Equivalent Units per Cost Element

topics.example: 200 units in process that are 25% complete equal 50 fully completed equivalent units.
remember: Equivalent units express work done on partial units in terms of equivalent finished units.
mistakes: Assuming the percentage of completion is always identical for material, labour, and overheads.

quiz.q: If 400 units are 60% complete with respect to conversion cost, their equivalent completed units are:
Equivalent production units concept is essential because:
o: All units in process are always 100% complete
Production is continuous and unfinished units exist at period end
It eliminates the need to record overhead costs
It converts abnormal loss into normal loss
quiz.why: It allows accurate unit cost calculation by converting partly finished units into equivalent full units.

topics.title: Steps in Process Costing
explain: Step 1: Analyse physical flow of production units (inputs and outputs reconciliation).
Step 2: Calculate equivalent units of production for each cost element.
Step 3: Collect and determine total cost for each cost element.
Step 4: Compute cost per equivalent unit by dividing total element cost by equivalent units.
Step 5: Assign total accumulated costs to completed output and ending work-in-process.

flow.title: Five Steps of Production Cost Report Preparation
steps: Assign Costs to Goods and Ending WIP

topics.example: Reconciling 10,000 input units into 9,000 finished output units and 1,000 ending WIP units before computing unit cost.
remember: Physical input units must always equal total physical output units (including losses and WIP).
mistakes: Dividing total process cost directly by physical units instead of equivalent units when WIP is present.

quiz.q: What is the first step in preparing a process production cost report?
o: Analysing the physical flow of production units
Crediting scrap value to process account
quiz.why: Step 1 requires tracking and reconciling physical units entering and leaving the process.

quiz.q: How is cost per equivalent unit calculated in Step 4?
o: Total Cost divided by Total Physical Input Units
Total Element Cost divided by Equivalent Units for that element
Ending WIP Cost divided by Completed Units
Total Scrap Value divided by Normal Loss Units
quiz.why: Cost per equivalent unit is total cost of an element divided by equivalent units determined for that element.

topics.title: Process Costing Methods: FIFO vs Weighted Average
explain: Under FIFO method, work required to complete opening WIP is calculated separately from fresh inputs.
In FIFO, closing work-in-process is valued strictly at current period's production cost.
Under Weighted Average method, opening WIP costs and current period costs are combined together.
In Weighted Average, total combined cost is divided by total equivalent units (opening WIP + fresh production).

flow.title: Choosing Valuation Method for WIP
steps: Identify Opening WIP Units and Costs
OR Apply Weighted Average (Blend Opening & Current Costs)
Value Finished Stock and Closing WIP

topics.example: Under FIFO, if opening WIP is 60% complete, only 40% additional work is counted in current period equivalent units.
remember: FIFO keeps previous period costs separate; Weighted Average averages old and new costs together.
mistakes: Including the already completed work percentage of opening WIP in FIFO equivalent unit calculation.

quiz.q: Under the FIFO method of process costing, opening WIP equivalent units are based on:
o: Work already completed in previous period
Remaining work required to complete the units in current period
quiz.why: FIFO only counts work done during the current period to complete opening WIP (100% minus % completed earlier).

quiz.q: When Weighted Average method is used, opening inventory costs are:
o: Aggregated with current costs to compute average unit cost
quiz.why: Weighted Average merges opening inventory costs with new costs incurred during the period.

topics.title: Inter-Process Profits
explain: Inter-process profit occurs when output of one process is transferred to next process at a profit-added transfer price instead of pure cost.
This system converts each process into an independent profit centre to measure operational efficiency.
It facilitates comparison between internal process cost and prevailing market price.
Unrealised profit contained in unsold closing stock must be deducted to show true cost for balance sheet purposes.

flow.title: Inter-Process Profit Transfer Mechanism
steps: Debit Next Process at Transfer Price
Eliminate Unrealised Profit from Closing Stock

topics.example: Process I transfers goods costing ₹44,200 to Process II at a transfer price of ₹54,000 (including ₹13,500 profit margin).
remember: Transfer price can be set as cost plus percentage profit or at fair market value.
mistakes: Failing to calculate and eliminate the unrealised profit reserve in closing stock at year-end.

quiz.q: Why are transfers between processes sometimes made at a price above cost?
o: To evaluate performance by treating each process as a profit centre
quiz.why: Inter-process profit allows management to measure efficiency and profitability of each process independently.

quiz.q: The main disadvantage of inter-process profits is that:
o: It introduces unrealised profit in closing stock requiring adjustment
It reduces the actual selling price of finished goods
quiz.why: Unsold stock contains profit credited before final sale, which creates unrealised profit complications.

topics.title: Operation Costing
explain: Operation Costing is a hybrid costing method combining features of job costing and process costing.
Used when products have different raw material inputs but undergo identical conversion operations.
Material costs are accumulated by job or batch order.
Conversion costs (labour and overheads) are accumulated by department or operation using predetermined application rates.

flow.title: Operation Costing Structure
steps: Track Material Costs by Specific Job/Batch
Sum Material & Conversion Costs for Final Unit Cost

topics.example: Shoe manufacturing where leather types differ per batch, but cutting, stitching, and soling operations are identical.
remember: Also known as Hybrid Product Costing System.
mistakes: Confusing operation costing with pure process costing where both materials and conversion are uniform.

quiz.q: Operation Costing is also commonly referred to as:
quiz.why: Operation costing blends job-order material tracking with process-style conversion cost accumulation.

quiz.q: In Operation Costing, conversion costs are accumulated by:
quiz.why: Conversion costs (labour and overheads) are collected by department or operation because activities are similar across variants.
